title: The Mississippi Marathon and the Problem with Education “Miracles”
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio argues that education's habit of celebrating miracles, from Atlanta's cheating scandal to the Mississippi literacy story, mistakes inflated or illusory results for genuine progress and avoids the slow work of building systems. He engages Rachel Canter's Progressive Policy Institute paper, which reframes Mississippi's early-literacy gains as a marathon built on clear standards and assessments, real consequences, evidence-based instruction and sustained implementation support. He notes that Mississippi's accountability infrastructure predates its reading reforms, so the gains were not a single policy shift. He observes that each camp, whether phonics, high-quality instructional materials or accountability, reads Mississippi as proof of its own priors, and he admits the case challenges his own skepticism of accountability. His conclusion is that the lesson is process, coherence and persistence rather than a transferable answer.
points: Calling a result a miracle excuses us from studying the conditions that produced it, since miracles are by definition not replicable.
Mississippi's gains rest on four interlocking elements introduced over years, and the accountability system came before the literacy reforms.
Education debates over Mississippi are shaped by confirmation bias, with every reform camp crediting its favorite lever.
The author concedes that accountability, inside a coherent system with instructional support, may help create performance and not merely measure it.
Durable improvement comes from aligning what schools are asked to do with what they are equipped to do, and then sticking with it.
quotes: I’ve said it for years about education: Show me a miracle and I’ll show you a scandal. That’s not cynicism, it’s pattern recognition.

Worse, “miracle” stories are not a corrective to education’s fad-driven culture, they are symptomatic of it. Both depend on the premise that success lies not in the slow work of building systems, but in the one magical lever we have somehow failed to discover and pull.

Her paper fills in the missing context. Mississippi’s progress rests on four interlocking elements: clear standards and assessments; real consequences for failure; a shift toward evidence-based instruction; and sustained support for implementation. Just as important, these elements did not arrive all at once. Canter’s timeline shows that Mississippi’s accountability infrastructure predates its literacy reforms—a sequencing that suggests these gains were not the product of a single policy shift, but of a system built over time.

Indeed, calling Mississippi a “miracle” is a kind of dismissal. It allows us to marvel at the outcome without taking seriously the conditions that produced it. Miracles, after all, are not meant to be replicated. That’s why they’re miracles.

Mississippi uncomfortably challenges my priors because is it suggests something I’d prefer not to concede so easily: that accountability, under the right conditions, may not just measure performance—it may help create it. When it’s part of a coherent system aligned with instruction, support, and clear expectations, it may play a more constructive role than its critics, myself included, sometimes imagine.
In sum, the real lesson of Mississippi is not that we’ve found The Answer. It’s that there may not be an answer, only a process: Coherence. Persistence. Political will and durability.
A marathon is not inspiring because it is miraculous. It’s inspiring because it is repeatable—and because so few of us have the discipline to run one.
